metaDescription: Six corded electric dethatcher-scarifiers priced under $300, compared on motor amps, width, depth settings and bag size for small to mid-size lawns.
expertTake: The SENIX 15-inch 13-amp is the best overall pick for its width, spring-steel tines and big bag. The EWORK 14-inch is the value pick if the lawn is small. Anyone with more than a third of an acre of heavy thatch should rent a gas power rake instead of forcing a corded machine through it.
introParagraphs: A dethatcher is a corded rake: a spinning reel of flexible tines drags dead grass and moss out of the lawn surface so water, air and seed can reach the soil. At this budget nearly every machine is a 2-in-1 that also carries a blade reel for light scarifying.

The cap here is $300, and prices move, so it reflects listing prices when this guide was updated. Within that limit the real differences are motor current, working width, how many depth positions you get, and how quickly the bag fills.

products.name: SENIX 15-Inch 13 Amp 2-in-1 Dethatcher
products.description:
The SENIX is built around a 15-inch reel carrying 24 spring-steel tines at 1.5 mm gauge, which is a heavier wire than the thin tines on the cheapest machines. Thicker wire resists bending when it meets a root flare or a buried sprinkler head, and it flicks thatch upward into the bag instead of just combing it flat. The 13-amp motor is rated for sustained load rather than a peak figure, which matters because thatch drags the reel down more than clean grass does.

Compared with the 14-inch Greenworks, the SENIX covers about seven percent more ground per pass and holds 13.2 gallons against a smaller bag, so you stop to empty it less often. The trade is weight and storage footprint: it is the biggest machine in this price bracket and needs a proper wall hook or shelf. Depth is a four-position lever, coarser than the five-step levers on the Sun Joe, so fine tuning on uneven turf takes a test strip.

Ownership is simple. Clear the tines after every session, check the reel nut for tightness, and rinse the bag so damp thatch does not mildew. Spring-steel tines can be unbolted and replaced individually, which is cheaper than a new reel. It is a good fit for lawns up to roughly a quarter acre where the thatch layer is moderate.
products.bestFor: Quarter-acre lawns with a moderate thatch layer where fewer passes and fewer bag stops matter.
pros: Heavier 1.5 mm spring-steel tines resist bending on roots
15-inch path cuts passes versus 13 and 14 inch rivals
Large 13.2 gallon bag means fewer stops
13-amp motor holds speed in dense thatch
cons: Largest and heaviest machine here, awkward to store
Four depth positions are less fine than five-step rivals

products.name: EWORK 14-Inch 12 Amp Dethatcher Scarifier
products.description:
The EWORK is the cheapest machine in this lineup and it earns the Best Value badge by offering the same basic architecture as machines costing noticeably more: a 12-amp motor, a 14-inch reel and a removable bag. The listing warns that the body is 22 inches wide at its widest while the working path is 14 inches, so check gate and shed-door clearance before assuming it fits through a narrow side yard.

Power is the compromise. A 12-amp motor has less reserve than the 13-amp SENIX or the 15-amp WEN, so on a lawn with a thick spongy mat you will need to take shallower passes and go over the area twice instead of one deep pass. That is slower but not damaging, and for lawns under about 3,000 square feet the extra time is small.

Because it is the newest and least established brand here, owner support and replacement-tine availability are the questions to ask before buying. Keep the spare hardware and take a photo of the reel layout before the first teardown. As a first dethatcher for a small yard it is a sensible low-risk purchase.
products.bestFor: Small lawns and first-time buyers who want the lowest entry cost.
pros: Lowest priced machine in this lineup
Dual dethatching and scarifying functions in one body
12-amp motor draws less from a shared circuit
Included grass catcher simplifies cleanup
cons: Body is far wider than its 14-inch path
Brand has a shorter record, so confirm tine availability

products.name: Westinghouse 13-Inch 12 Amp Dethatcher
products.description:
Westinghouse sells the same platform in a 13-inch and a 16-inch version, and this is the narrower one. It carries 20 spring tines on the dethatching reel and 16 blades on the scarifier reel, spinning at up to 3,300 RPM from a 12-amp motor. The reel is smaller than the SENIX, so it turns faster for its size but removes less per pass.

The narrow path is the point. It maneuvers around beds, tree rings and fence corners where a 15 or 16-inch machine would have to be tilted and scalp the edge. If your lawn is chopped into small areas, a 13-inch head will finish with fewer awkward turns than the wider models, even though the straight runs are longer.

Expect to swap reels with a few bolts rather than a tool-free latch, and keep the blade reel away from stones. At this price tier it is a plain, predictable machine, with the usual caveat that the 12-amp motor wants shallow passes in heavy thatch.
products.bestFor: Yards divided by beds, trees and tight corners.
pros: 13-inch head fits between beds and tree rings
Up to 3300 RPM reel keeps tines whipping at speed
Includes both tine and blade reels
Same platform has a wider sibling if you outgrow it
cons: Narrow path means more passes on open lawns
12-amp motor has little reserve in heavy thatch

products.name: Sun Joe AJ798E 12.6-Inch 12 Amp Dethatcher
products.description:
The Sun Joe AJ798E offers a five-position depth lever, the finest control among the narrow 12-amp machines here. Five steps matter on lawns that are not billiard-table flat, because you can raise one notch over a crowned patch instead of scalping it. The tines are spring steel shaped to move air, which helps carry loosened thatch into the removable 8-gallon bag.

That bag is the limitation. Eight gallons fills quickly on a thick mat, and against the 13.2 gallons on the SENIX you will be walking to the compost pile far more often. The 12.6-inch path is also the narrowest on the list, so this is a machine for small areas more than a half-day project.

Sun Joe is a long-established brand with widespread parts and manuals, which is a real ownership advantage at this price. Plan on hosing the bag clean, checking the cord strain relief, and storing it dry. A reliable choice where fine depth adjustment is more valuable than raw width.
products.bestFor: Uneven small lawns where fine depth steps prevent scalping.
pros: Five depth positions give finer height control
Established brand with accessible parts and manuals
Removable bag keeps cleanup straightforward
Reel moves air as well as scraping thatch
cons: 8-gallon bag fills fast in thick thatch
Narrowest cutting path of the group

products.name: Greenworks 14-Inch 13 Amp Dethatcher Scarifier
products.description:
Greenworks centers its design on convenience. A quick-release mechanism swaps the dethatching and scarifying attachments without hunting for a wrench, and a push-button start replaces the safety-bail pattern on some rivals. A 13-amp motor in a 14-inch body gives a good balance of power to width.

The depth control has only three positions, the coarsest of the group. That is fine for flat turf but a limitation on rolling ground, and the SENIX at four steps or the Sun Joe at five will give you more precision. Greenworks also describes the machine as lightweight and easy to maneuver, which suits owners who lift it into a trunk or carry it up steps.

The brand ranks among the more recognizable names in garden power tools, so replacement tines and bags are easier to find than for lesser-known imports. Clean the attachments after each use and check the quick-release latch for debris. A solid mid-range choice when swapping reels is a regular chore.
products.bestFor: People who switch between raking and scarifying and want a tool-free change.
pros: Quick-release attachment swap needs no tools
13-amp motor in a compact 14-inch body
Push button start is easy on the hand
Recognizable brand with accessible spares
cons: Less width than 15 or 16 inch machines

products.name: Westinghouse 16-Inch 15 Amp Dethatcher
products.description:
The 16-inch Westinghouse is the strongest machine in this under-$300 lineup, pairing a 15-amp motor turning up to 3,500 RPM with 24 spring tines and a 20-blade scarifier head. Five depth settings from -0.5 to +0.25 inch span the full range from skimming moss to cutting shallow grooves for overseeding.

Sixteen inches of width plus the extra current make it the machine to pick for the largest or thickest lawn on this list. The cost is on the circuit side: 15 amps is the most a standard household circuit can handle before the breaker trips, so use a heavy outdoor extension cord, ideally 14 gauge or thicker, and do not share the circuit with anything else.

Compared with its 13-inch sibling it takes about a quarter fewer passes on open turf, and compared with the SENIX it has finer depth control. It is also the heaviest feeling in use, and the long cord is the main hazard near the reel. Rinse the tines, store the machine dry and replace bent tines early.
products.bestFor: Larger or thatchier lawns that need the most motor and width under the cap.
pros: 15-amp motor has the most reserve of the group
Five depth positions from -0.5 to +0.25 inch
16-inch path covers open turf quickly
Both tine and blade reels included
cons: Needs a heavy gauge cord and a dedicated circuit
Heaviest to carry and store of the lineup

buyingCriteria.explanation: On a corded tool the rating is current draw, not horsepower, so a 15-amp motor has more potential than a 12-amp one but also uses most of a household circuit. Thatch drags the reel down much more than clean grass, so reserve matters: the 15-amp Westinghouse 16-inch has about a quarter more headroom than the 12-amp EWORK. Buyers often assume more RPM equals more power, but RPM without torque just means a fast stall.

Width sets how many passes a lawn needs, but wider machines also demand more motor and a bigger bag. The 16-inch Westinghouse covers about 23 percent more ground per pass than the 13-inch version of the same machine. On tight, bed-heavy yards the narrow 13-inch head wins because the wide ones scalp edges when tilted.

Depth is the setting that decides whether you remove thatch or damage the crown of the grass. Three positions on the Greenworks is the minimum; five positions on the Sun Joe AJ798E or the Westinghouse 16-inch let you adjust by a small step on a crowned patch. Always make the first pass at the shallowest setting and step down only if thatch remains.

Spring-steel tines flex over obstacles and spring back, while thin wire bends and stays bent. The SENIX specifies 1.5 mm tines, a concrete thickness number most listings leave out. Carbon steel rusts if stored wet, so wipe the reel dry after each use and replace tines individually when they bend.

A bag that fills in ten minutes turns a one-hour job into a two-hour one. The SENIX at 13.2 gallons holds over 60 percent more than the Sun Joe at 8 gallons. Plan to empty bags often regardless, and expect a lot of volume: a thatched lawn can fill a dozen bags of debris.

A thin extension cord causes voltage drop, which makes the motor run hot and stall under load. Use a 14-gauge outdoor cord for runs of 50 feet or less and heavier beyond that, and keep the cord behind you when working. The 15-amp machines are especially sensitive since they use almost the entire circuit capacity.

specDecoder.meaning: The current the motor draws at full load. Higher amps usually means more torque, until the circuit limit.
specDecoder.watchFor: The 12-amp EWORK and 15-amp Westinghouse 16 differ by three amps, a real gap in thick thatch.

specDecoder.meaning: Reel speed with no load. Under load it drops, and loaded speed is what rakes thatch.
specDecoder.watchFor: The 3,500 and 3,300 RPM figures on the Westinghouse pair are no-load numbers.

specDecoder.meaning: The path the reel clears per pass. It is not the same as the machine's overall body width.
specDecoder.watchFor: The EWORK lists a 14-inch path but a 22-inch body, so measure your gate.

specDecoder.meaning: How many steps the height lever has. More steps give finer control on uneven ground.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Greenworks offers three steps while the Sun Joe AJ798E and Westinghouse 16 offer five.

specDecoder.meaning: The machine ships with a tine reel for dethatching and a blade reel for scarifying.
specDecoder.watchFor: Blade reels cut roughly a few millimetres into soil, which is much lighter than a dedicated gas scarifier.

howWeEvaluated.title: Motor and width balance
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared amp rating against cutting width, because a wide reel on a weak motor stalls in thick thatch. The 13-amp SENIX at 15 inches and 15-amp Westinghouse at 16 inches scored highest here. The 12-amp machines scored lower for heavy work but remain fine for light annual maintenance.

howWeEvaluated.title: Depth adjustment range
howWeEvaluated.description: We read each spec sheet for number of depth steps and range. Five-position levers on the Sun Joe AJ798E and the Westinghouse 16 earned more credit than the three steps on the Greenworks. Fine control reduces scalping risk.

howWeEvaluated.title: Tine and reel construction
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked whether tines are spring steel and what gauge is stated. The SENIX is the only one that states a 1.5 mm gauge. Replaceable individual tines were rated above sealed reels.

howWeEvaluated.title: Collection and cleanup
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed bag volume, since the 13.2 gallon SENIX bag and 8 gallon Sun Joe bag lead to very different job lengths. We also considered how easily bags remove and empty.

howWeEvaluated.title: Owner feedback patterns
howWeEvaluated.description: We evaluated owner feedback patterns for common failure points such as reel nuts working loose, thin cords, and difficulty finding spare tines. Established brands like Sun Joe and Greenworks gained points for spares availability.

cards.label: 12 amp
cards.text: The EWORK, Westinghouse 13-inch and Sun Joe AJ798E run on 12 amps. They draw less, cost less and are fine for light thatch if you make shallow, repeated passes.

cards.label: 15 amp
cards.text: The Westinghouse 16-inch has the most reserve and cuts deeper in one pass, but demands a heavy cord and an uncluttered circuit.

howToChoose.note: Choose 12 amps for light annual care on small lawns, and 15 amps if thatch is thick or the lawn is large.

howToChoose.subheading: For Moss and Heavy Thatch Specifically

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Look for 15 amps or at least 13 amps, a bag over 12 gallons, and stiff spring-steel tines. Make the first pass at the shallowest setting and repeat if needed.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Westinghouse 16-inch and SENIX are best here: the Westinghouse for pure motor, the SENIX for bag size and 1.5 mm tines.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Your lawn exceeds a third of an acre, you dethatch every year, or you want the Westinghouse 16-inch and its 15-amp motor over the EWORK.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: The lawn is small and thatch is light, in which case the EWORK or Westinghouse 13-inch will do the job once a year.

maintenance.why: Damp thatch packs between tines and rusts them. A stiff brush clears it in a minute.
Vibration loosens fasteners. A loose reel nut can damage the shaft.
Bent tines drag unevenly and shred turf. Replace them individually.
Wet debris left in the bag grows mildew. Dry it before storing.
Cuts in the cord are a shock hazard. Replace damaged cords.

faq.q: What is the difference between dethatching and scarifying?
faq.a: Dethatching uses flexible tines to pull loose thatch from the surface. Scarifying uses rigid blades to cut shallow grooves into the soil, which helps overseeding. Most machines here do both by swapping reels.

faq.q: Can I get a good electric dethatcher for under $300?
faq.a: Yes. Every machine here has an electric motor of 12 to 15 amps and a bag, and prices move, so the cap reflects listing prices when this guide was updated. The limit is the lack of a gas engine for very large lawns.

faq.q: How long do these machines last?
faq.a: With rinsing, dry storage and replacing bent tines, a corded unit can run for many seasons. Most failures come from loose reel hardware, damaged cords or overloaded motors.

faq.q: Does more RPM mean better dethatching?
faq.a: Not necessarily. RPM is the no-load speed and drops under thatch. Torque and tine design matter more than the headline RPM number.
Dethatch while grass is actively growing: early fall for cool-season grasses, late spring for warm-season. Soil should be moist but not soaked.

faq.q: How do I know if my lawn needs dethatching?
faq.a: Cut a small wedge out with a spade. If the spongy brown layer is thicker than about half an inch, dethatch. A thinner layer is healthy.
